publication.title: Data Quality Based Intelligent Instrument Selection with Security Integration
publication.publisher: Journal of Data and Information Quality
publication.abstract: We propose a novel Data Quality with Security (DQS) integrated instrumentation selection approach that facilitates aggregation of multi-modal data from heterogeneous sources. As our major contribution, we develop a framework that incorporates multiple levels of integration in finding the best DQS-based instrument selection: data fusion from multi-modal sensors embedded into heterogeneous platforms, using multiple quality and security metrics and knowledge integration. Our design addresses the security aspect in the instrumentation design, which is commonly overlooked in real applications, by aggregating it with other metrics into an integral DQS calculus. We develop DQS calculus that formalizes the problem of finding the optimal DQS value. We then propose a Genetic Algorithm–based solution to find an optimal set of sensors in terms of the DQS they provide, while maintaining the level of platform security desirable by the user. We show that our proposed algorithm demonstrates optimal real-time performance in multi-platform instrument selection. To facilitate the framework application by the instrumentation designers and users, we develop and make available multiple Android applications.

publication.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
publication.abstract: Abstract Given n robots contained within a square grid surrounded by four walls, we ask the question of whether it is possible to move a particular robot a to a specific grid location b by performing a sequence of global step operations in which all robots move one grid step in the same cardinal direction (if not blocked by a wall or other blocked robots). We show this problem is NP-complete when restricted to just two directions (south and west). This answers the simplest fundamental problem in uniform global unit tilt swarm robotics. We then consider a relaxed version of this problem in which the goal is to move a robot a to a specific row regardless of its horizontal placement. We show that if asking about the bottom-most row of the square grid, then this version of the problem is solvable in polynomial time. Finally, we discuss several areas for future research and open problems.

publication.abstract: During every Atlantic hurricane season, storms represent a constant risk to Texan coastalcommunities and other communities along the Atlantic coast of the United States. A storm surgerefers to the abnormal rise of sea water level due to hurricanes and storms; traditionally, hurricanestorm surge predictions are generated using complex numerical models that require high amountsof computing power to be run, which grow proportionally with the extent of the area covered bythe model. In this work, a machine-learning-based storm surge forecasting model for the LowerLaguna Madre is implemented. Robust Autonomous Vehicle Computer-Vision-Based Localization in Challenging Environmental Conditions
publication.abstract: In this paper, we present a novel autonomous vehicle (AV) localization design and its implementation, which we recommend to employ in challenging navigation conditions with a poor quality of the satellite navigation system signals and computer vision images. In the case when the GPS signal becomes unstable, other auxiliary navigation systems, such as computer-vision-based positioning, are employed for more accurate localization and mapping. However, the quality of data obtained from AV’s sensors might be deteriorated by the extreme environmental conditions too, which infinitely leads to the decrease in navigation performance. To verify our computer-vision-based localization system design, we considered the Arctic region use case, which poses additional challenges for the AV’s navigation and might employ artificial visual landmarks for improving the localization quality, which we used for the computer vision training. We further enhanced our data by applying affine transformations to increase its diversity. We selected YOLOv4 image detection architecture for our system design, as it demonstrated the highest performance in our experiments. For the computational platform, we employed a Nvidia Jetson AGX Xavier device, as it is well known and widely used in robotic and AV computer vision, as well as deep learning applications. Our empirical study showed that the proposed computer vision system that was further trained on the dataset enhanced by affine transformations became robust regarding image quality degradation caused by extreme environmental conditions. It was effectively able to detect and recognize images of artificial visual landmarks captured in the extreme Arctic region’s conditions. The developed system can be integrated into vehicle navigation facilities to improve their effectiveness and efficiency and to prevent possible navigation performance deterioration.

Study on Destructive Informational Impact in Unmanned Aerial Vehicles Intergroup Communication
publication.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel approach to formalize the impact of malicious intergroup informational attacks toward a group of unmanned aerial vehicles communication. Infrequent but critical situations arise when an already authorized group member starts to transmit false data to other group participants. These scenarios can be caused by a software or hardware malfunction or a malicious attack, and cannot be prevented by the conventional security measures. The impact of such actions can be critical for a group’s performance. To address this issue, we develop and formalize the model of unmanned aerial vehicles’ intergroup communication and provide the calculus for a group’s performance destructive impact. We employ a multi-agent-based approach to formalize the information interaction between the participants of the unmanned aerial vehicles group. The model we propose possesses such properties as symmetry and scalability, as it considers individual participants as separate homogeneous distributed agents that have to perform their tasks in parallel to achieve the joint group goal. We classify informational threats by the type of the destructive impact they cause: apparent and hidden. Data contained in informational messages is categorized according to the agent’s destructive impact premeditation degree: intentional and unintentional. To verify the model proposed, we conduct an empirical study. The results show that the false data transmitted during the intergroup communication adversely affects the group’s performance, and such an impact can be measured and quantified.

publication.title: A Study of Human Balance and Coordination Using a Head Mounted Display
publication.publisher: Journal of Computers and Information Science in Engineering
publication.abstract: This paper investigates the hypothesis that men and women perform differently in virtual environments in terms of balance and coordination during surprise events. It reports on an experiment in human subject balance and coordination using an HTC Vive head-mounted display (HMD) to create a virtual environment. For the experiment, 30 male and 30 female subjects of college age were asked to navigate along a clear path in a virtual world using a controller with their dominant hand and asked to balance a virtual ball on a virtual plate using the other controller in the nondominant hand. The test subjects moved along a clearly marked path, with three surprise obstacles occurring: a large rock landing near the path, an explosion near the path, and a flock of birds coming across the path. Data included six degrees-of-freedom (DOF) trajectories for the head and both hands, as well as data gathered by the computer system on ball location and velocity, plate location and velocity, and ball status. Likert scale questionnaires were answered by the test subjects relative to video game experience, sense of presence, and ease of managing the ball movement. Statistics showed that the male students dropped the ball less frequently at p = 0.0254 and p = 0.0036. In contrast, female students were aware of their performance with correlation levels of 0.632 and 0.588.

publication.abstract: Forecasting of natural disasters such as inundations can be of great help for emergency bodies and first responders. In coastal communities, this risk is often associated with storm surge. To produce flood forecasts for coastal communities a system must incorporate models capable of simulating such events based on forecasted weather conditions. In this work, a system for forecasting inundations based predominantly on storm surge is explored. An automation and coupling strategy were implemented to produce forecasted flood maps automatically. The system leverages an ocean circulation model and a channel water flow model to estimate flood events in South Texas specially alongside the Lower Laguna Madre. The system around the models is implemented using Python and the meteorological forcing input is obtained from weather forecasting models maintained by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The forecasted weather data retrieval, data processing and automation of the models is successful, and the complete stack of software can be deployed locally or in cloud solutions to accelerate computations. The resulting system performs as expected and successfully produces flood maps automatically.

publication.title: Deciphering the Role of Ion Channels in Early Defense Signaling against Herbivorous Insects
publication.abstract: Plants and insect herbivores are in a relentless battle to outwit each other. Plants have evolved various strategies to detect herbivores and mount an effective defense system against them. These defenses include physical and structural barriers such as spines, trichomes, cuticle, or chemical compounds, including secondary metabolites such as phenolics and terpenes. Plants perceive herbivory by both mechanical and chemical means. Mechanical sensing can occur through the perception of insect biting, piercing, or chewing, while chemical signaling occurs through the perception of various herbivore-derived compounds such as oral secretions (OS) or regurgitant, insect excreta (frass), or oviposition fluids. Interestingly, ion channels or transporters are the first responders for the perception of these mechanical and chemical cues. These transmembrane pore proteins can play an important role in plant defense through the induction of early signaling components such as plasma transmembrane potential (Vm) fluctuation, intracellular calcium (Ca2+), and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, followed by defense gene expression, and, ultimately, plant defense responses. In recent years, studies on early plant defense signaling in response to herbivory have been gaining momentum with the application of genetically encoded GFP-based sensors for real-time monitoring of early signaling events and genetic tools to manipulate ion channels involved in plant-herbivore interactions. In this review, we provide an update on recent developments and advances on early signaling events in plant-herbivore interactions, with an emphasis on the role of ion channels in early plant defense signaling.

publication.title: On the effects of hierarchical self-assembly for reducing program-size complexity
publication.abstract: In this paper we present a series of results which show separations between the standard seeded model of self-assembly, Winfree's abstract Tile Assembly Model (aTAM), and the “seedless” 2-Handed Assembly Model (2HAM), which incorporates the dynamics of hierarchical self-assembly. In particular, we focus on the problem of self-assembling various shapes while minimizing the sizes of tile sets, or “programs”, in each of these models in order to compare and contrast the models. A high-level overview of a subset of these results was presented in a paper by the authors in STACS 2013, but in this version we expand and improve the set of results related to showing separations between the two models according to their abilities to self-assemble various shapes. We exhibit classes of finite shapes that can be self-assembled more efficiently in each model. We also demonstrate infinite shapes that can self-assemble in one model but not in the other, as well as a shape which cannot self-assemble in either model.

publication.title: Infusing Raspberry Pi in Computer Science Curriculum for Enhanced Learning
publication.publisher: American Society for Engineering Education (ASEE) Conference, June 22-26, 2020
publication.city: Montreal, Quebec (Virtual Conference due to COVID-19)
publication.abstract: Abstract— With the advent of cloud computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and mobile computing, CS faculty are continuously revamping the curriculum material to address such burgeoning set of technologies in practical and relatable ways. Raspberry Pi (RPi) devices represent an ideal hardware/software framework that embodies all these technologies through its simple architecture, small form factor (that minimizes the volume and footprint of a desktop computer), and ability to integrate various sensors and actuators that network together and connect to the Cloud. Therefore, one of the strategies of Computer Science Department, to enhance depth of learning concepts, has been to infuse Raspberry Pi (RPi) in computer science courses. RPi has been incorporated since 2017 in targeted courses, notably, Computer Organization & Assembly Language, Computer Architecture, Database Management Design & Implementation, Unix/Linux Programming, Internet Programming, and Senior Project. An inexpensive credit card sized computer, an RPi lends itself to allow depth of learning of concepts. From implementing firewalls,intrusion detection systems, scripting, client-server based computing, distributed computing, to interfacing with sensors and actuators, a student is guided to polish concepts taught in a class through RPi Project Based Learning (RPBL). Computer science curriculum already provides breadth of learning. The infusion of RPi in key courses provides depth in targeted concepts. There are peripheral desirable consequences as well, including a student learning prevalently used Linux environment even though a targeted course may have nothing directly to do with Linux.Furthermore, RPi provides an opportunity for students to realize that software programs can be interfaced with sensors and actuators to provide immersed experience in programming. From simply interfacing a switch and a Light Emitting Diode (LED) to getting data from sensors,buffering, and uploading to the cloud, a student already would have touched upon multiple disciplines in computer science. This paper provides a blueprint to infusing RPi in the targeted courses, and how each RPi based project provides depth to a targeted concept. Index Terms—Raspberry Pi, Cloud Computing, Internet of Things (IoT), Mobile Computing, Linux.

publication.abstract: Infrastructure is a significant factor in economic growth for systems of government. In order to increase economic productivity, maintaining infrastructure quality is essential. One of the elements of infrastructure is roads. Roads are means which help local and national economies be more productive. Furthermore, road damage such as potholes, debris, or cracks is kin to many on-road accidents that have cost the lives of many drivers. In this paper, we propose a system that uses Convolutional Neural Networks to detect road degradations without data pre-processing. We utilize the state-of-the-art object detection algorithm, YOLO detector for the system. First, we developed a basic system working on data collecting, pre-processing, and classification. Secondly, we improved the classification performance achieving 97.98% in the overall model testing, and then we utilized pixel-level classification and detection with a method called semantic segmentation. We were able to achieve decent results using this method to detect and classify four different classes (Manhole, Pothole, Blurred Crosswalk, Blurred Street Line). We trained a segmentation model that recognizes the four classes mentioned above and achieved great results with this model allowing the machine to effectively and correctly identify and classify our four classes in an image. Although we obtained excellent accuracy from the detectors, these do not perform particularly well on embedded systems due to their network size. Therefore we opted for a smaller, less accurate detector that will run in real-time on a cheap embedded system, like the Google Coral Dev Board, without needing a powerful and expensive GPU.

publication.abstract: With the advance of sensor technologies, the Multivariate Time Series classification (MTSC) problem, perhaps one of the most essential problems in the time series data mining domain, has continuously received a significant amount of attention in recent decades. Traditional time series classification approaches based on Bag-of-Patterns or Time Series Shapelet have difficulty dealing with the huge amounts of feature candidates generated in high-dimensional multivariate data but have promising performance even when the training set is small. In contrast, deep learning based methods can learn low-dimensional features efficiently but suffer from a shortage of labelled data. In this paper, we propose a novel MTSC model with an attentional prototype network to take the strengths of both traditional and deep learning based approaches. Specifically, we design a random group permutation method combined with multi-layer convolutional networks to learn the low-dimensional features from multivariate time series data. To handle the issue of limited training labels, we propose a novel attentional prototype network to train the feature representation based on their distance to class prototypes with inadequate data labels. In addition, we extend our model into its semi-supervised setting by utilizing the unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on 18 datasets in a public UEA Multivariate time series archive with eight state-of-the-art baseline methods exhibit the effectiveness of the proposed model.

publication.title_secondary: International Conference on Unconventional Computation and Natural Computation
publication.abstract: The algorithmic self-assembly of shapes has been considered in several models of self-assembly. For the problem of shape construction, we consider an extended version of the Two-Handed Tile Assembly Model (2HAM), which contains positive (attractive) and negative (repulsive) interactions. As a result, portions of an assembly can become unstable and detach. In this model, we utilize fuel-efficient computation to perform Turing machine simulations for the construction of the shape. In this paper, we show how an arbitrary shape can be constructed using an asymptotically optimal number of distinct tile types (based on the shape’s Kolmogorov complexity). We achieve this at O(1) scale factor in this straightforward model, whereas all previous results with sublinear scale factors utilize powerful self-assembly models containing features such as staging, tile deletion, chemical reaction networks, and tile activation/deactivation. Furthermore, the computation and construction in our result only creates constant-size garbage assemblies as a byproduct of assembling the shape.

publication.abstract: According to recent security analysis reports, malicious software (a.k.a. malware) is rising at an alarming rate in numbers, complexity, and harmful purposes to compromise the security of modern computer systems. Recently, malware detection based on low-level hardware features (e.g., Hardware Performance Counters (HPCs) information) has emerged as an effective alternative solution to address the complexity and performance overheads of traditional software-based detection methods. Hardware-assisted Malware Detection (HMD) techniques depend on standard Machine Learning (ML) classifiers to detect signatures of malicious applications by monitoring built-in HPC registers during execution at run-time. Prior HMD methods though effective have limited their study on detecting malicious applications that are spawned as a separate thread during application execution, hence detecting stealthy malware patterns at run-time remains a critical challenge. Stealthy malware refers to harmful cyber attacks in which malicious code is hidden within benign applications and remains undetected by traditional malware detection approaches. In this paper, we first present a comprehensive review of recent advances in hardware-assisted malware detection studies that have used standard ML techniques to detect the malware signatures. Next, to address the challenge of stealthy malware detection at the processor’s hardware level, we propose StealthMiner, a novel specialized time series machine learning-based approach to accurately detect stealthy malware trace at run-time using branch instructions, the most prominent HPC feature. StealthMiner is based on a lightweight time series Fully Convolutional Neural Network (FCN) model that automatically identifies potentially contaminated samples in HPC-based time series data and utilizes them to accurately recognize the trace of stealthy malware. Our analysis demonstrates that using state-of-the-art ML-based malware detection methods is not effective in detecting stealthy malware samples since the captured HPC data not only represents malware but also carries benign applications’ microarchitectural data. The experimental results demonstrate that with the aid of our novel intelligent approach, stealthy malware can be detected at run-time with 94% detection performance on average with only one HPC feature, outperforming the detection performance of state-of-the-art HMD and general time series classification methods by up to 42% and 36%, respectively.

grant.abstract: Measuring teaching performance is a key indicator to assess teaching quality because teaching behaviors reflect how well teachers understand subject matter, design learning tasks for students, are equipped with strategies for facilitating learning, and implement the designed learning tasks to class. When it comes to implementing a lesson plan, gathering students’ attention is the first step in implementing the lesson plan to help students process information about a subject topic. Efficient delivery of a concept maximizes learning experiences. Although we recognize the importance of evaluating teaching performance, evaluating teaching performance is costly. Especially, analyzing teaching behaviors in research takes painful efforts and needs arduous manual work, since it includes video recording, developing rubrics, transcribing, coding various teaching behaviors including verbal and nonverbal behaviors, analyzing the data, and so forth. Aligned with data-driven empirical studies, this study seeks an innovative way to calibrate teaching quality by analyzing teaching behaviors with deep learning supported by Artificial Intelligence (AI). Here, from a multidisciplinary approach based on theories in cognition, learning sciences, and computer sciences, we attempt to build an AI-driven system which calibrates teaching quality by analyzing teachers’ behaviors that help students deeply engage in learning. An AI system will be trained based on machine learning algorithms and the data obtained from the system will be cross-checked with the findings from manual coding to test and secure the system’s reliability. This automated system makes an attempt to build one of the first tools that analyze teaching behaviors driven by AI. The findings from the project will lay a foundation to measure various teaching behaviors for classroom orchestration and learning behaviors more accurately and efficiently.

grant.abstract: Overview: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) proposes to establish the “CREST Center for Multidisciplinary Research Excellence in Cyber-Physical Infrastructure Systems (MECIS).” The Center’s mission is to advance and transform the much-needed research and education at the nexus of automation, sensors, and artificial intelligence (AI), as integral parts of the “NSF’s 10 Big Ideas,” anticipating the revolutionary cyber-physical infrastructure systems (CIS). Three Colleges of Engineering, Sciences, and Education at UTRGV in collaboration with the Universities of Illinois (at Urbana-Champaign and at Chicago) and California (Riverside) will pursue multidisciplinary research on CIS, aiming to: (i) transfer technology to various transportation, logistics, manufacturing, and construction industries; and (ii) prepare a minority STEM workforce to drive future CIS-based communities. The Center envisions a portfolio of three research subprojects on automation, sensors, and AI that bridges diverse STEM disciplines. A holistic, multi-level approach is adopted to address CIS planning, design, and operation. While each subproject constitutes a unique element, their synergy ensures the CIS integrity. Subproject 1 pushes the frontiers of knowledge in future transportation infrastructure, which will be transformed by autonomous vehicles (AVs) and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), in six directions: (i) at the planning level, public acceptance and policy issues of (U)AV; (ii-iv) at the design level, computer vision, automatic navigation, and model/field-based testing of the designed capabilities; and (v, vi) at the operation level, human-(U)AV interactions and network-wide inter-(U)AV interactions. Subproject 2 designs and embeds sensors in CIS for two purposes. First, (U)AV sensors help perform automated tasks. Second, sensors in civil infrastructure and (U)AVs monitor infrastructure health. Three research areas are defined: (i, ii) at the design level, computational simulation, synthesis, and 3D printing of sensor materials and UAV structures, and (iii) at the operation level, cost-effective decision-making to upkeep infrastructure health using sensor data. Since (U)AVs and sensors will inherently generate big data, Subproject 3 will synchronously work with subprojects 1 and 2 to: (i) develop AI solutions for big data management, and (ii) develop AI algorithms for big data analytics and decision making in the design and operation of (U)AVs and infrastructure. UTRGV is the nation’s second largest Hispanic-Serving Institute (HIS) located in South Texas with an established record of preparing underrepresented minority students for STEM careers. The Center will provide (under)graduate students with cutting-edge CIS research experience, will integrate CIS research and education, and will pave a pathway from High School through graduate programs in STEM disciplines. This broad initiative at UTRGV will also offer new courses related to the subprojects. The Center will further enhance the research infrastructure at UTRGV and will strengthen the research competitiveness of a diverse group of faculty. Intellectual Merit: The proposed self-sustaining Center will play a key role in transforming the scientific discoveries at the intersection of automation, sensors, and AI technologies, which are the integral elements of next-generation CIS. The Center will address current gaps in the planning, design, and operation of CIS by proposing innovative theoretical, computational, experimental, and empirical solutions spanning from micro (molecule)- to macro (system)-scale, which also yield practical solutions valuable for the industry. Broader Impacts: The Center’s research and education activities will develop an underrepresented workforce equipped with the skills to address complex societal problems. The Center will partner with the public and private sectors to advance technology transfer and product development in CIS. The Center’s activities are key for the establishment of an inaugural engineering doctoral program, which will be vital in elevating UTRGV to a Research I institution and advancing the CIS research agenda in a predominantly HSI. The Center's research findings will be made available to the research community as journal publications and conference proceedings, which will inform other domains undergoing related transformations, such as the health industry, manufacturing and production systems, and the military.

grant.abstract: Computational knowledge and skills have become essential to all disciplines and economic sectors. The ubiquity of computing impacts how we educate and prepare the future workforce regardless of one’s chosen career pathway. Thus, it is imperative to develop non-CS undergraduate students’ essential skills in solving problems computationally in their discipline and in possessing knowledge of ethical concerns related to growing cyber threats and vulnerabilities. To address this need, three institutions of higher education are collaborating as a Networked Improvement Community [NIC]: The University of Texas at El Paso [UTEP], Texas A&M University Corpus Christi, and the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley. The aim of improvement at each institution is to raise non-CS students’ motivation to pursue knowledge of computational skills and become aware of ethical and security issues. The proposed project has three objectives to meet its goal of developing non-CS students’ skills for solving problems using computation: (1) develop and refine outcome-focused, problem-based, discipline-relevant course modules for creating course sequences that are adaptable to varying institutional context and disciplinary degree programs; and (2) incorporate inclusive practices into delivery of the modules to retain and advance students in the computational sequence. Intellectual Merit. UTEP is the lead institution and Alliance Backbone of the NSF-funded National CAHSI (Computing Alliance for Hispanic-Serving Institutions) INCLUDES Alliance. The Alliance aims to broaden participation of Hispanics in computing using the conditions of collective impact, an improvement science framework closely aligned with NICs. With its 12-year history of building and supporting academic partnerships, CAHSI and its Backbone team are well positioned to support the IHE partnership in the proposed work, which aligns with CAHSI’s mission of growing and sustaining a networked community focused on advancement of Hispanics in computing. The proposed project has defined a collection of modules focused on problem-solving, computational thinking, cybersecurity, and ethics that can be used to create a sequence for STEM, non-CS majors that is adaptable to local context. In addition, the Alliance Backbone will support the professional development of instructors involved in the project with evidence- and research-based inclusive practices, which are especially important for success of Hispanics and other individuals from underrepresented groups. Using the improvement science framework with feedback from the external evaluator, the investigators and STEM subject matter experts from the partner institutions will critically review and iteratively improve organizational structures, course modules, and sequences. The investigators have expertise in working with interdisciplinary projects and are committed to collaborate in refinement of a reconfigurable, introductory course sequence designed to prepare the future STEM workforce with computational knowledge and skills. Broader Impacts. The partner institutions are Hispanic-Serving Institutions [HSIs] with majority Hispanic populations. Working with non-CS departments, the project will serve a significant number of women who are over-represented in the partnerships’ STEM fields (other than Physics) involved in the project. This has potential to broaden participation of students from underrepresented groups in computing, a priority of the NSF. The proposed modules are adaptable across STEM and non-STEM disciplines. Because the Alliance operates as a network of networks, it has numerous outlets for disseminating modules to both Alliance institutions and other HSIs. One such outlet is the Alliance’s non-profit-organization partners, Excelencia in Education and Great Minds in STEM, that are national Hispanic organizations sharing a core purpose of increasing the number of Hispanics who are competitive in higher education generally and in computing specifically.

grant.abstract: Getting students’ interest piqued in a college degree in a STEM field is challenging. However, due to ever increasing pace of technology transformation, the area of computer science is frequently afforded an opportunity to attract students to relatively new areas with visible impact on everyday life and business. Cyber security, a field pervasively touching almost every aspect of modern life, boasts a promise of job growth of 28% from 2016 through 2026 according to BLS. On the other hand, according to ISACA, 84% of organizations believe that only half or fewer of the applicants for security jobs are qualified. This proposal is for enhancing Teaching and Research Utilizing Security Track based on a Versatile Integrated Lab for Learning Enrichment (TRUSTVILLE). The proposed integrated security lab, which includes Internet of Things (IOT) equipment as well, will be familiarizing students with the state of the art cyber security appliances and software in a realistic environment to give them a competitive edge in the job market for serving to fill the existing gap in cyber security in public and private sectors. The Computer Science Department at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley has been offering courses in cyber security area, however, a formal cyber security track with the required training has not been offered due to lack of hardware and software. The institution has Data, Intelligence and Security (DIS) group, with its own lab space, and prides itself for hosting the first International Conference on Data, Intelligence and Security (ICDIS) in April 2018. Given the current faculty expertise in cyber security, experience in teaching related courses, having a DIS group with its own lab space and the market potential for cyber security jobs, the university is strategically poised for offering a specialized track in cyber security to enhance teaching and research. Due to the market demand, the hardware and software related with cyber security are expensive, and this proposal is for securing funds to assist the institution’s ongoing efforts to establish a market driven cyber security track supported by a modern cyber security integrated laboratory. Since low traffic volume is encountered in a lab environment, expensive high-performance ASIC based hardware is not needed. However, the updates to the firmware and software of security hardware, and to the software itself could be as frequent as daily, for example, to block vulnerabilities including zero-day worms. Therefore, most of the expense of cyber security integrated lab is not in the hardware, but rather in the annual subscription of the software to keep the lab current. The cyber security track in computer science will consist of seven computer science courses geared towards cyber security, three criminal justice courses, and a senior cornerstone project in the area of cyber security. All of these courses will incorporate Project Based Learning (PBL) methodology to familiarize the students with industry grade cyber security tools and appliances. The required integrated laboratory will consist of a gamut of cyber security related hardware and software to understand and analyze the weaknesses of systems and procedures and learn how to strengthen security at different levels. The integrated security laboratory will consist of software and hardware such as IoT devices, IPS, IDS, threat hunting, vulnerability management, traffic monitoring, penetration testing, forensics, encryption, network security and endpoint security for both on premise and cloud assets.

grant.title: AF: Small: RUI: Unifying Self-Assembly Through Tile Automata
grant.abstract: Self-assembly is the bottom-up process by which simple, unorganized components autonomously combine to form larger, more complex structures. This process is abundant in nature, and is a key underlying mechanism for the construction of biological organisms. Researchers are also turning to self-assembly technology for the precise design of ever smaller and more complex nanoscale devices. Thus, self-assembly is emerging as a fundamental tool for nanotechnology. Of particular interest is algorithmic self-assembly in which local interactions between objects carry out sophisticated computation to efficiently assemble target shapes and patterns. Fully understanding the power and control of self-assembly systems presents the possibility of designing molecular algorithms for precise and efficient manipulation of matter at the nanoscale. A number of experimentally motivated models of algorithmic self-assembly have been proposed with different efficiencies and capabilities. Developing theory towards a better understanding of these models is the focus of this project. In this proposal the PIs propose a framework for unifying the diverse set of established, experimentally motivated models of algorithmic hierarchical self-assembly. The proposed framework involves the introduction of a mathematically abstracted model of algorithmic self-assembly termed Tile Automata that combines the geometric growth of 2-handed self-assembly, as seen within a number of tile self-assembly models, with local state changes rules, as seen in cellular automata systems such as Conway's Game of Life. This project aims to develop fundamental lemmas and theorems within this model to grow the Tile Automata framework into a powerful tool for proving surprising results within more complex but experimentally motivated models, as well as prove connections between previously distinct models by way of constant-scale simulation results. In tandem with the theoretical projects depicted in this proposal, a major goal of this project is to increase research participation among students at the University of Texas - Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and increase the number of UTRGV undergraduate and masters students who enroll in computer science Ph.D. programs. This project details ongoing plans to use student-focused research seminars aimed at introducing and retaining undergraduate student participation and co-authorship. The project further details a number of additional outreach activities aimed at engaging undergraduate researchers, such as the formation of a research-focused hackathon termed Hack-Research, which the PIs plan to deploy here at UTRGV as a part of this project. The PIs have a proven track record of using research seminars to foster student participation in research. Further, the merger of UT-Pan American and UT-Brownsville to form UT-Rio Grande Valley has yielded the largest Hispanic-serving institution in the United States, where both PIs are located. Thus, this project offers a rare opportunity to make a substantial impact on broadening participation among under-represented minority groups in the field of Computer Science. DNA self-assembly technology is emerging as a powerful tool to manipulate matter at the nanoscale. This tool could be applied to various practical applications such as the mass fabrication of nanoscale devices or molecular computing. Further, self-assembly is a fundamental phenomenon that dictates how complex organisms can grow from simple molecules, implying that further understanding of self-assembly helps in understanding some of nature's greatest mysteries. The University of Texas - Rio Grande Valley, located in the South Texas Rio Grande Valley area, has more than 30,000 students, with a 90% Hispanic and 55% female student population. UTRGV, is the largest Hispanic-serving institution in the US. A primary goal of this proposal is to increase the research activity of UTRGV Computer Science students by developing a large portion of the orignal research for this proposal within the environment of student-centered research seminars. The PIs also plan to expand participation in research by initiating a new style of research-focussed hack-a-thon at UTRGV. Due to the nature of the UTRGV student body, these plans will help broaden participation in post-graduate Computer Science among under-represented minority groups.

grant.title: "An Expert Systems Approach to Feature Recognition for Marine ROV Operation with Virtual Reality"
grant.abstract: During the Summer of 2017, the MSI (Minority Serving Institution) team collaborated with a Maritime Security Center (MSC) Summer Research Institute (SRI) team at Stevens Institute of Technology to develop a low-cost Virtual Reality interface to assist with the operation of an ROV (Remote Operated Vehicle) for maritime homeland security applications. The proposed research extends this work by adding an expert system for feature recognition to assist with the operation of marine ROVs. Expertise is provided by Dr. Englot from the MSC at Stevens Institute to the U. of Texas-Rio Grande Valley team, and this expertise is used to develop an expert system that can recognize features such as contraband (drugs, etc.) and IEDs (Improvised Explosive Devices) that may attached to the hull of ships or placed underwater on pier pilings or other harbor structures. The methods include classic expert system techniques including: the development of software to manipulate the expertise and interface with the user, elicitation of expertise from a human expert (Dr. Englot), testing of the expert system performance, and documentation of results with the intention to transition this work to an operational application of interest to relevant DHS components. Through the development and demonstration of this VR (Virtual Reality) system with expert feature recognition, new capabilities are developed that directly support US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) efforts to keep our ports and harbors safe, and eliminate the smuggling of contraband (drugs, etc.). Currently, ROVs have a significantly poor man-machine interface, and this research offers an opportunity to begin to correct this deficiency, providing better security for our homeland.

grant.abstract: Automatic target recognition (ATR) system based on the machine learning technology can automatically extract features from a moving target using its inverse synthetic aperture radar (ISAR) images for high-speed target. However, ATR systems have not been applied for the widespread use in high-speed weapon system due to the difficulty in evolving to learn to recognize new targets. In this project, we propose fast target recognition based on efficient ISAR image classification methods using ISAR image generated from the realistic 3D moving target model. It consists of three modules, multiple mono-static and/or bi-static ISAR imaging, 3D reconstruction for radar images, and complex valued 3D convolutional neural network.

grant.abstract: Hurricane storm surge is an abnormal rise in sea level that destroys coastal lands due to the extensive eroding caused by the rapid flow circulation of a hurricane, as well as overland floods caused by the abnormal rise in the ocean. The storm surge is a definite threat to the Lower Laguna Madre (LLM), though it was fortunately spared by Hurricane Harvey. LLM plays a significant role as part of the United State Gulf Intracoastal Waterway by providing tourist attraction and natural habitats for marine life. A storm surge will not only damage the natural and man-made environment, but will impair the Texas economy as well. To fill the information gap regarding the impact of a hurricane storm surge on coastal inundation, we need more accurate and realistic prediction of storm surge flood event. We propose coupling the hurricane storm surge and watershed flood models by using the storm surge heights computed by the storm surge model as input data to the watershed flood model. The major outcomes of this proposed project consist of (1) improved coastal flood interactive GIS maps incorporating hurricane storm surge, (2) coupled hydrodynamic model to be used for the LLM hurricane storm surge and flow circulation prediction, and (3) improved local emergency evacuation routes based on coastal flood maps. The immediate benefit of these outcomes to the end-users are (1) high fidelity coastal flood geospatial information that will serve as an effective tool for local emergency management and planning and (2) robust numerical models that will be applicable to flow circulation prediction, flood routing, and traffic capacity simulation.

grant.title: System for Predicting South Padre Island shoreline Erosion
grant.abstract: We propose developing a numerical prediction system to estimate shoreline changes and dune erosion impacted by time scales of coastal storm events and arbitrary geometry alterations for coastal infrastructures. The system will compute coastal morphodynamic processes of ocean sediment transport, sand dune deformation, and cross sectional profile changes. The processes will be estimated based on hydrodynamic model computations of short/long wave transformation and dynamic currents, as well as hurricane storm surge and coastal inundation. We are proposing to build the morphodynamic computational model by using the XBeach model, which is a public domain numerical code developed by open source community with major funding from U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, UNESCO-IHE, and Deltares. With existing supports of the TGLO CMP #23 program, we will develop the hydrodynamic model of the South Padre Island vicinity area. To improve the modeling efficiency, we will couple the XBeach coastal morphodynamic model with the hydrodynamic model. The coupled model will maximize computational accuracy of shoreline changes and dune erosion during hurricane storm surge along the 32.2 miles of South Padre Island.

grant.title: Complexity, Scale, and Benchmarks in Algorithmic Self-Assembly
grant.abstract: Self-assembly is a bottom-up process in which simple, unorganized components autonomously combine to form large, complex structures. This process is found throughout nature as a key underlying mechanism for the construction of biological organisms. Researchers are also turning to self-assembly as a method for the precise design of complex nanoscale devices, making self-assembly an emerging technique in nanotechnology. Of particular interest is algorithmic self-assembly in which local interactions between objects carry out sophisticated computation to efficiently assemble target shapes and patterns. Fully understanding the power and control of self-assembly systems presents the possibility of designing molecular algorithms for precise and efficient manipulation of matter at the nanoscale. The goal of this project is to develop the mathematics of abstract self-assembly models that are motivated by experimental reality. As these systems are computationally universal, this mathematical study lies in the intersection of mathematics and computer science. In this proposal the PIs present a research plan to explore the capabilities and complexity of a family of mathematical models of tile-based self-assembly motivated by current technology in DNA nanotechnology. This exploration centers around three types of problems (combinatorial, algorithmic, and complexity-theoretic) that each characterize these models in distinct ways. Preliminary results in these three areas provide new ideas for future efforts, including the resolution of long-standing open problems in the field. We complement this theoretical focus with preliminary wet lab results and proposed future experiments. In tandem with the theoretical projects depicted in this proposal, a major goal of this project is to increase research participation among students at the University of Texas - Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and increase the number of UTRGV undergraduate and masters students who enroll in computer science Ph.D. programs. This project details ongoing plans to use student-focused research seminars aimed at introducing and retaining undergraduate student participation and co-authorship. The PIs have a proven track record with utilizing such seminars to foster student participation in research. Further, the merger of UT-Pan American and UT-Brownsville to form UT-Rio Grande Valley has yielded the largest Hispanic-serving institution in the United States, where all three PIs are located. Thus, this project offers a rare opportunity to make a substantial impact on broadening participation among under-represented minority groups in the field of Computer Science. DNA self-assembly technology is emerging as a powerful tool to manipulate matter at the nanoscale, and has a broad range of practical applications, including the mass fabrication of nanoscale devices and molecular computing. On the other hand, self-assembly is a fundamental phenomenon that dictates how complex organisms can grow from simple molecules, and further understanding of self-assembly helps in understanding some of nature's greatest mysteries. The University of Texas - Rio Grande Valley, located in the South Texas Rio Grande Valley area, has more than 30,000 students, with a 90% Hispanic and 55% female student population. UTRGV, is the largest Hispanic-serving institution in the US. A primary goal of this proposal is to increase the research activity of UTRGV Computer Science students by developing a large portion of the theory and experimental research for this proposal within the environment of student-centered research seminars. The PIs plan to further develop current research seminars to involve a larger number of students in original research. Due to the nature of the UTRGV student body, this plan will help broaden participation in post-graduate Computer Science among under-represented minority groups.

grant.title: Complexity, Scale, and Benchmarks in Hierarchical Self-Assembly
grant.abstract: Self-assembly is the bottom-up process by which simple, unorganized components autonomously combine to form larger, more complex structures. This process is abundant in nature, and is a key underlying mechanism for the construction of biological organisms. Researchers are also turning to self-assembly technology for the precise design of complex nanoscale devices [5, 45, 46, 53, 65, 76, 83, 93], making self-assembly an emerging tool for nanotechnology. Of particular interest is algorithmic self-assembly in which local interactions between objects carry out sophisticated computation to efficiently assemble target shapes and patterns. Fully understanding the power and control of self-assembling systems enables the possibility of precise, efficient, and algorithmic manipulation of matter at the nanoscale. Developing models and theory towards this goal that are closely tied to experimental reality is the focus of this project. In this proposal, we present a research plan to explore the novel capabilities available to three models of hierarchical tile-based self-assembly motivated by current experimental technology. In hierarchical tile assembly, initial system monomers combine to form larger and more complex polymers that, in turn, act as monomers that combine into even larger polymers. Our preliminary results demonstrate that the novel capabilities of hierarchical models imply techniques and results impossible in traditional non-hierarchical or seeded models of tile assembly. We complement this theoretical focus with preliminary wet lab results and proposed future experiments, as well as software development projects. In tandem with the theoretical and experimental work proposed, a major goal of this project is to increase research participation among students at the University of Texas - Rio Grande Valley and increase the throughput of undergraduate and masters students who pursue careers in computer science research, including continuing on to Ph.D. programs. This project details ongoing plans to encourage such participation based on student-focused research seminars aimed at introducing and retaining undergraduate student participation and co-authorship. The merger of UT-Pan American and UT-Brownsville to form UT-Rio Grande Valley has yielded the largest Hispanic-serving institution in the United States, where all three PIs are located. Thus, this project offers a rare opportunity to make a substantial impact on broadening participation among under-represented minority groups in the field of Computer Science.

grant.title: Developing Randomization and Alberization for Algorithms and Complexity Theory
grant.abstract: Computational theory serves as the backbone of Computer Science, providing a large number of fundamental mathematical tools which underpin Computer Science’s many sub-fields. However, as its tool set has matured and expanded, so has the influence of computational theory. This synergistic combination serves to make it even more important to continue the pursuit of fundamental advances in computational theory and the tools it provides to its ever broadening sphere of influence. In this proposal, the PIs demonstrate a plan for making great strides in further developing two such newly emerging and important tools, randomization and algebrization. While randomness has long been viewed as a nuisance in mathematics and something to be avoided or minimized, extremely powerful methods of harnessing its power for the design of randomized algorithms have recently cast it in a whole new light. Randomization has allowed for the creation of extremely powerful and efficient algorithms that were otherwise unobtainable. Another tool, algebrization, provides methods for the reformulation of a diversity of problems into forms in which the highly developed tools of algebra can be brought to bear on them. These two sets of tools provide a powerful platform from which to attack a broad and important set of crucial open problems on the boundaries of computational complexity and algorithmic development, and the PIs form a group of scientists uniquely qualified to attack and solve these problems. One target is the further development of the theory of testing monomials in multivariate polynomials. The complexity portion of research in this area was initiated by the PIs, and the resultant theory has found applications in areas such as graph algorithms, Bioinformatics, and wireless networking. The complexity aspects of the monomial testing problem and its variants will be extensively investigated with two objectives. One is to understand how this problem may be related to critical problems in complexity, and if so to what extent. The other is to exploit possibilities of applying algebraic properties of polynomials to the study of those problems. Of particular interests are separations among fundamental complexity classes. Secondly, the PIs plan to use randomized and algebraic methods to tackle a set of problems in the field of exact and parameterized tractable computation, an active and developing field in recent years. By applying randomized and algebraic techniques, the PIs will develop faster exact and parameterized algorithms for, and study lower bounds of, a set of well-known graph problems (e.g. the Hamiltonian cycle problem). Another direction of the work consists of studying problems in the field of computational learning theory which are closely related, and amenable, to the techniques of randomization and algebrization. The two PIs work in the same department, have very strong research records in each of the areas listed above, have great familiarity with the tools of randomization and algebrization, have worked closely together on a large set of successful collaborations, and continually maintain close ties through research projects and seminars. This combination puts them in a position to make important advances across the wide range of the projects proposed. Intellectual merit of the proposed activities: Randomization is a basic tool of algorithm design applicable to many problems. Algebrization has significant importance in both algorithm design and computational complexity theory. As this proposal combines algebrization with randomization, the results of the proposed research will make new contributions to the core area of computational theory and discover new applications in the fields of Bioinformatics and computational learning theory. It is anticipated that new algebraic and derandomization techniques will be developed for testing monomials and the results thereof may lead to possible breakthroughs in areas of complexity class separation and parameterized computation. Broader impacts of the proposed activities: The University of Texas-Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV), located in the South Texas Rio Grande Valley area, has more than 28,000 students. UTRGV is the largest university in the US to have a majority Hispanic student population: 90% of its students are Hispanics, including 59% females. An important part of this proposal is to support underrepresented minority and female graduate and undergraduate students. We plan to develop a randomized computation course and propose a set of applied algorithm projects for both undergraduate and graduate students at UTRGV. These will attract participation of female and male engineers/scientists from the Hispanic community to pursue research in Computer Science. The training and experiences obtained by those students through the proposed research endeavors will lay a stepping-stone for them to land at fruitful careers in areas of science, technology, engineering and mathematics.

presentation.abstract: Measuring teaching performance is a key indicator to assessing teaching quality because teaching behaviors reflect how well teachers understand a subject matter, design learning tasks for students, are equipped with strategies for facilitating learning, and implement the designed learning tasks in class. When it comes to implementing a lesson plan, gathering students’ attention is the first step in implementing the lesson plan to help students process information about a subject topic. Efficient delivery of a concept maximizes learning experiences. Although we recognize the importance of evaluating teaching performance, evaluating teaching performance is costly. This study seeks an innovative way to calibrate teaching quality by analyzing teaching behaviors with deep learning supported by Artificial Intelligence (AI). Here, from a multidisciplinary approach based on theories in cognition, learning sciences, and computer sciences, we attempt to build an AI-driven system that calibrates teaching quality by analyzing teachers’ behaviors that help students deeply engage in learning.

presentation.title: Polynomial Simulations of CRN Models with Trimolecular Void Step-Cycle CRNs
presentation.event: 22nd International Conference on Unconventional Computing and Natural Computing
presentation.abstract: We investigate the computational power of Step-Cycle Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs) when restricted to void reactions of size at most $(3,1)$.Step-Cycle CRNs extend the previously introduced step CRN model by repeatedly cycling through a fixed sequence of species additions and reaction phases. We show that even under the severe constraint of trimolecular void rules --- which can only delete or preserve species --- the model retains full computational power. In particular, we prove that (3,1) void Step-Cycle CRNs can polynomially simulate (1) any general CRN, (2) any general Step CRN, and (3) any general Step-Cycle CRN.

presentation.title: Reachability in Deletion-only Chemical Reaction Networks
presentation.event: 31st International Conference on DNA Computing and Molecular Programming
presentation.abstract: For general discrete Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs), the fundamental problem of reachability-the question of whether a target configuration can be produced from a given initial configuration-was recently shown to be Ackermann-complete. However, many open questions remain about which features of the CRN model drive this complexity. We study a restricted class of CRNs with void rules, reactions that only decrease species counts. We further examine this regime in the motivated model of step CRNs, which allow additional species to be introduced in discrete stages. With and without steps, we characterize the complexity of the reachability problem for CRNs with void rules. We show that, without steps, reachability remains polynomial-time solvable for bimolecular systems but becomes NP-complete for larger reactions. Conversely, with just a single step, reachability becomes NP-complete even for bimolecular systems. Our results provide a nearly complete classification of void-rule reachability problems into tractable and intractable cases, with only a single exception.

presentation.abstract: The prediction of inundations due to hurricane storm surge can be of great help for first responders andthe general public. The accurate forecast of inundations will require a system capable of working 24/7,have high standards of reliability and be stable. In case of a storm event the forecasting system willprovide a reliable and accurate data source for flooding maps. A flood forecasting system requires thelatest forecasting data regarding wind speed, direction and surface level pressure. The forecasting datathat will be used in this project is obtained from NOAA, more specifically, from the North AmericanMesoscale Forecasting System (NAM); a model that produces gridded forecasting data over NorthAmerica. The retrieved data from NAM needs to be processed before it can be used. The gridded dataneeds to be trimmed, interpolated onto a regular grid and processed to fit the input parameters for themodels involved. The models used for inundation prediction need to be coupled and automated to fitthe requirements of the project. The models that will be used are ADCIRC and HEC-RAS. These models,when coupled, will output the necessary data to create flooding maps. This data needs to be handledand superimposed onto an interactive base GIS map, which will be available for the public to access.The system will be constructed using popular tools for data processing and automation built on Python. In this way,the public will possess reliable forecasting flood maps and will be able to plan their actions ahead of unpredictable catastrophic disasters.
